sections.h2: Why Incoterms are strategic in B2B
p: Incoterms define how responsibilities, risks and costs are shared between seller and buyer along the supply chain. In a B2B environment, they drive operational control, cost visibility and contractual alignment with partners (suppliers, forwarders, insurers).

A clear understanding of Incoterms helps prevent disputes, optimise final price and speed up decision-making. In a volatile market, the goal is not just to “pay the lowest price”, but to secure the reliability and predictability needed to keep your flows running.

sections.h2: Overview of Incoterms 2020 relevant to sea freight
ul: EXW (Ex Works) — The seller makes goods available on their premises. The buyer takes care of transport, formalities and risk from pickup.
FCA (Free Carrier) — The seller delivers the goods to the buyer's carrier at an agreed place.
FOB (Free On Board) — Maritime specific: risks pass to the buyer when the goods are loaded on board at the port of departure.
CFR (Cost and Freight) — The seller pays main carriage to the port of arrival; risk passes at loading.
CIF (Cost, Insurance and Freight) — The seller pays freight + minimum insurance to the port of arrival.
DAP/DPU/DDP — Delivery at destination up to the consignee’s premises (depending on the variant), with extended seller responsibilities.

sections.h2: FOB vs CIF: balancing control and predictability
p: FOB gives the buyer control over main carriage (choice of carrier, contracts, tracking). It can bring savings and performance if internal logistics capabilities are mature.
CIF provides budget predictability (freight and insurance borne by the seller) and reduces coordination efforts on the buyer side, at the cost of less direct control over transport.

ul: Delivery: the point at which the seller formally delivers the goods to the buyer (defined by the Incoterm)
Risk transfer: the exact moment when risk passes from seller to buyer
Main costs: sea freight and surcharges (BAF/CAF/PSS)
Customs formalities: export/import responsibilities according to the chosen Incoterm
Insurance: ad valorem coverage recommended to protect cash flow

p: As a general rule: FOB/CFR/CIF transfer risk at loading; DAP/DPU/DDP move the delivery point to the country of arrival; EXW/FCA shift a large part of upstream responsibilities to the buyer.
ul: FOB: seller handles export; buyer pays main carriage and insurance; risk passes at loading
CFR: seller handles export + main carriage; risk passes at loading for the buyer
CIF: seller handles export + freight + insurance; risk passes at loading for the buyer
DAP: seller pays transport to the site; import formalities are handled by the buyer
DDP: seller covers the full chain up to delivery, duties & taxes included

p: Transit times vary (Le Havre/Antwerp ↔ Luanda). For regular flows to Angola, FOB suits experienced importers who can negotiate freight and optimise CBM. CIF brings administrative comfort when speed of execution and budget visibility are priorities.
Under CIF, the minimum Institute Cargo Clauses (C) coverage is not always enough. For B2B flows, ad valorem insurance is recommended to protect business continuity.
Documentary compliance (invoice, packing list, certificates of origin) must fully match the Incoterm to limit customs risks.

sections.h2: Frequent mistakes and how to avoid them
ul: Confusing delivery point with risk transfer point
Failing to adjust insurance when risk transfers early (FOB/CFR)
Document inconsistencies (quantities, weights, descriptions) leading to delays
Choosing an Incoterm that does not reflect internal logistics maturity

Check documentary adequacy and insurance coverage

faq.q: FOB vs CIF: what is the difference in practice?
faq.a: FOB: the seller bears costs/risks up to loading on board. CIF: includes cost, insurance and freight to the port of arrival. In B2B, CIF offers predictability on total cost, while FOB offers more control for the importer.

faq.q: Which Incoterms should I prefer for imports on the France–Angola corridor?
faq.a: In practice, most B2B imports on the France–Angola corridor use FOB or CIF. FOB suits experienced importers who want to choose their own carrier, negotiate rates directly and keep control over main carriage. CIF is more comfortable for companies that prioritise budget predictability and a single point of contact on the seller’s side. In all cases, we compare several scenarios (FOB, CFR, CIF and sometimes DAP) on total delivered cost for your container flows before recommending a setup.
They do not change regulations, but define who is responsible for procedures and at which point.

faq.q: Do Incoterms affect liability in case of damage?
faq.a: Yes. They define where risk passes from seller to buyer. Proper insurance and documentary evidence are essential.

faq.q: Can I change Incoterm during negotiation?
faq.a: Yes, provided it is clearly stated in the contract and the impacts on price, schedule and insurance are taken into account.
No. FCA is better suited to non-maritime transport up to delivery to the carrier; FOB is specific to sea freight with risk transfer at loading on board.
Convenient for the buyer but demanding for the seller (tax, import). It should be used only when you have strong local capabilities.
